paragraphs.heading: Reading climate in wood
paragraphs.text: Dendroclimatology is the study of past climates using trees, mostly by looking at the rings they add each year. A ring grows wide in a year when conditions suit growth and narrow when times are hard. From rings, scientists have worked out the climate of many single places going back hundreds or even thousands of years. By pooling many tree-ring studies, sometimes alongside other climate proxy records, they have also estimated past climates for whole regions and the globe.

paragraphs.heading: Why rings work so well
paragraphs.text: Ring width is not the only clue: other features, such as maximum latewood density (MXD), have proved better stand-ins for climate. Rings can also be dated well through dendrochronology, which means matching ring patterns from one sample to the next. That matching lets a record reach further back using dead trees, even wood from old buildings or archaeological digs. Each ring marks one year clearly, unlike other methods such as boreholes. And because rings respond to temperature, moisture and cloudiness, they can tell about more than heat alone, though that cuts both ways.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting out the causes
paragraphs.text: Many things besides climate shape a ring's width. Climate factors include temperature, precipitation, sunlight and wind; other factors include soil, the tree's age, fire, competition between trees, genes, logging, grazing animals, pests, disease and the level of CO₂. To pull these apart, scientists sample "limiting stands", groups of trees expected to respond mostly to the one factor they care about. At a mountain's upper treeline, trees are expected to track temperature more than precipitation, since there warmth is limited and water is in excess. At the lower treeline, the reverse is expected. The trick is imperfect, because several factors still act even at a limiting stand, but it helps.

paragraphs.heading: Cleaning up the signal
paragraphs.text: When a confusing factor varies at random from tree to tree or site to site, the best answer is simply more samples. A tree's age is handled with statistics, either by fitting spline curves to the whole record or by comparing trees of similar age across periods, called regional curve standardization. Choosing sites with care, such as places modern people have left alone, also limits some of the confusion. Researchers usually assume ring width changes in a straight line with the factor they study, but if that factor changes enough, the response can level off or even reverse. Anyone who has kept a house plant knows you can give it too little water or too much.

paragraphs.heading: The divergence problem
paragraphs.text: One puzzle is called the divergence problem. At many treeline sites in northern forests, thermometers show substantial warming, but the rings there show no matching change in maximum latewood density or, in some cases, width, so a trend drawn from those rings alone would show no substantial warming. The two temperature graphs part ways from the 1950s on, which gave the problem its name, though not every study finds it. This raises the question of whether similar mismatches happened before there were thermometers. Some evidence points to human activity as the cause, which would confine it to recent times, but using affected rings can make past temperatures look too high and so understate today's warming. Research on how to reconcile the two records continues.

paragraphs.heading: Where trees cannot help
paragraphs.text: Tree rings also have blind spots. They cannot be used to estimate polar or ocean climates. In very wet tropical regions, Australia and southern Africa, trees generally grow through the whole year and do not show clear yearly rings.
